regenerate.firstTitle: Multi-Digit Multiplication: Multiplying by a Single Digit
regenerate.newTitle: Multi-Digit Multiplication: Multiplying by a Single Digit

questions.prompt: When multiplying a multi-digit number by a single digit using the vertical algorithm, which digit should you multiply first?
options: The leftmost (highest place value) digit
The rightmost (ones place) digit
The middle digit
It doesn't matter which digit you start with

questions.prompt: In the problem 137 × 5, what do you do with the carried digit after multiplying the ones place?
options: Ignore it
Write it as part of the final answer immediately
Add it to the product of the next digit multiplication
Subtract it from the next digit's product

questions.prompt: When restacking a multiplication problem vertically, how should the numbers be arranged?
options: Smaller number on top, larger number on bottom
Larger number on top, single digit below it
Numbers side by side horizontally
Larger number on the left, single digit on the right

questions.prompt: In 2,617 × 4, when you multiply 4 × 6 (tens place) and get 24, plus any carried number, what do you do with the result if it is also two digits?
options: Write both digits in the same column
Write the ones digit in that column and carry the tens digit to the next column
Discard the tens digit
Write the result in the final answer without carrying

questions.prompt: Solve 137 × 5 using the vertical multiplication algorithm. Show your answer.
Solve 2,617 × 4 using the vertical multiplication algorithm. Show your answer.
Explain in your own words why carrying is necessary when multiplying multi-digit numbers by a single digit.
questions.answer: Carrying is necessary because when you multiply a digit by the single-digit number, the product can be two digits long (10 or greater). Since each column can only hold one digit in the final answer, the tens digit of that product must be carried over and added to the next column's multiplication result.

questions.prompt: Solve 426 × 3 using the vertical multiplication algorithm. Show your work and final answer.

newDraft.studentInstructions: Review the steps for multiplying a multi-digit number by a single digit. Then answer each question, showing your work for the short answer problems. Remember to multiply from right to left and carry when a product has two digits!
newDraft.title: Multi-Digit Multiplication: Multiplying by a Single Digit

regenerate.firstTitle: Understanding Fractions: Halves, Quarters, and Thirds
regenerate.newTitle: Understanding Fractions: Halves, Quarters, and Thirds

options: A whole number with no parts
A part of a whole made up of equal-sized pieces
A shape with four sides
A number used only for counting

questions.prompt: If a pizza is cut into 4 equal slices, what is each slice called?
options: A half
A third
A quarter
A whole

questions.prompt: In the fraction 1/3, what does the bottom number (3) tell you?
options: How many parts are being discussed
How many equal parts the whole is divided into
The size of the whole object
The number of wholes you have

questions.prompt: Which of the following is equal to one half (1/2)?
How many thirds make one whole?
Why can't a pizza cut into one big slice and one small slice be called halves?
options: Because there are only 2 pieces
Because the pieces are not equal in size
Because pizza can't be divided
Because halves must always be square

questions.prompt: Explain what the top number (numerator) in a fraction tells you.
questions.answer: The numerator tells you how many parts of the whole are being discussed or counted.

questions.prompt: If you cut a sandwich into 2 equal parts, what fraction does each part represent?
questions.answer: Each part represents one half, written as 1/2.

questions.prompt: Write the fraction that represents four quarters, and explain what it equals.
questions.answer: Four quarters is written as 4/4, and it equals one whole.

questions.prompt: Explain in your own words why the pieces of a whole must be equal in size to correctly call them halves, quarters, or thirds.
questions.answer: The pieces must be equal in size because a fraction describes equal parts of a whole; if the parts are different sizes, they cannot accurately be called halves, quarters, or thirds since each part must represent the same portion of the whole.

newDraft.studentInstructions: Read each question carefully. For multiple choice questions, circle the best answer. For short answer questions, write your answer in complete sentences using what you learned about halves, quarters, and thirds.
newDraft.title: Understanding Fractions: Halves, Quarters, and Thirds
